[a7 1/2] # SMS gateway

An SMS gateway is used to bridge between applications that need to send and/or receive SMS and a mobile network's Short Message

[a7 2/2] Service Center (SMSC[1]). As a result, SMS gateways provide a means of sending and receiving SMS between applications and mobile
>> p! a7 2

[a7 1/2] users.

In most cases, SMS and MMS are eventually routed to a mobile phone[2] through a wireless carrier. SMS gateways are commonly used as a

[a7 2/2] method for person-to-person to device-to-person (also known as application-to-person) communications. Many SMS gateways[3] support
>> p! a7 3

[a7 1/2] content and media conversions from email[4], push, voice, and other formats.

## Gateway types

edit[5]]

[a7 2/2] Several mobile telephone network operators have true fixed-wire SMS services. These are based on extensions to the European
>> p! a7 4
[a7 1/2] Telecommunications Standards Institute[6] (ETSI) Global System for Mobile Communications[7] (GSM) SMS standards and allow messaging between any

[a7 2/2] mix of fixed and mobile equipment. These use frequency-shift keying[8] to transfer the message between the terminal and the Short
>> p! a7 5
[a7 1/2] Message Service Center[9] (SMSC). Terminals are usually based on Digital Enhanced Cordless Telecommunications[10] (DECT), but wired handsets and

[a7 2/2] wired text-only (no voice) devices exist. Messages are received by the terminal recognising that the Caller ID[11] is that of the SMSC
>> p! a7 6

[a7 1/2] and going off-hook silently to receive the message.

## Implementations

edit[12]]

## GSM gateway appliance

edit[13]]

[a7 2/2] A direct-to-mobile gateway is a device equipped with built-in wireless GSM connectivity that enables SMS text messages to be sent and
>> p! a7 7
[a7 1/2] received directly via a mobile network. Messages can originate from email, web pages, or other software applications, using a unique identifier from

[a7 2/2] the mobile phone's Subscriber Identity Module (SIM card). Unlike SMS aggregators, which route messages through third-party networks,
>> p! a7 8
[a7 1/2] direct-to-mobile gateways are installed on an organization's own network and connect directly to a local mobile operator.

[a7 2/2] The connection is established by acquiring a SIM card from a mobile operator and installing it in the gateway. These appliances
>> p! a7 9
[a7 1/2] traditionally handle hundreds to thousands of messages per month, while modern devices can send up to 100,000 messages daily. Vendors that

[a7 2/2] historically provided GSM gateways for voice communications have expanded their offerings to include SMS capabilities.
>> p! a7 10
[a7 1/2] Advanced gateways often include features such as SIM management to control message volume per SIM, ODBC support to interface with databases, and HTTP

[a7 2/2] or SMPP interfaces for integration with third-party applications. They provide organizations with enhanced control over delivery,
>> p! a7 11
[a7 1/2] compliance, and reporting compared to traditional SMS aggregator services. Direct-to-mobile gateways are commonly used in scenarios requiring high

[a7 2/2] reliability and timely message delivery, such as transactional notifications, promotional campaigns, and operational alerts.
>> p! a7 12

[a7 1/2] ## Regulation

edit[14]]

GSM gateway equipment is covered by the Wireless Telegraphy Act[15] in the UK and can legally be used by any business

[a7 2/2] to send SMS to their own customers or prospects when using their own gateway equipment. In Canada, SMS gateway providers are regulated
>> p! a7 13

[a7 1/2] by the Canadian Wireless Telecommunications Association (CWTA/txt.ca).
In India, it is regulated by the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India[16]

[a7 2/2] (TRAI).
In Pakistan, it is regulated by the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority[17](PTA).

## Direct-to-SMSC

edit[18]]
>> p! a7 14
[a7 1/2] A direct-to-short message service centre[19] (SMSC) gateway is a software application, or a component within a software application, that connects

[a7 2/2] directly to a mobile operator's SMSC via the Internet or direct leased line connections. The Short Message Peer-to-Peer[20] (SMPP)
>> p! a7 15
[a7 1/2] protocol is typically used to convey SMS between an application and the SMSC. Direct-to-SMSC gateways are used by SMS aggregators to provide SMS

[a7 2/2] services to their clients and large businesses who can justify such use. They are typically employed for high volume messaging and
>> p! a7 16

[a7 1/2] require a contract directly with a mobile operator.

## Direct-to-SMS gateway

edit[21]]

[a7 2/2] An SMS gateway typically sits between the end-user who needs to send/receive SMS and a mobile network's SMSC. Such gateways provide
>> p! a7 17
[a7 1/2] their customers with a choice of protocols, including HTTP, SMTP, Short Message Peer-to-Peer[20] and Web Services. Providers of SMS gateway

[a7 2/2] services include SMS aggregators and mobile operators. SMS gateways are also available as part of messaging services such as AOL, ICQ
>> p! a7 18

[a7 1/2] and others.

In order to send/receive messages with mobile subscribers, an SMS gateway connects with (i) mobile network SMSCs and/or (ii) other SMS

[a7 2/2] gateways. It is, therefore, possible that an SMS gateway has a combination of connections with mobile network SMSCs and connections with
>> p! a7 19
[a7 1/2] other SMS gateways in order to provide its services. However, there is an increasing potential for delivery problems with SMS with increasing number

[a7 2/2] of SMS gateways in the delivery chain.

## Email clients

edit[22]]
>> p! a7 20
[a7 1/2] Text messages can be sent from a personal computer to mobile devices via an SMS gateway or Multimedia Messaging Service[23] (MMS) gateway, using

[a7 2/2] the most popular email client[24] programs, such as Outlook, Thunderbird, and so on. The messages must be sent in ASCII[25]
>> p! a7 21
[a7 1/2] "text-only" mode. If they are sent in HTML mode or using non-ASCII characters, they will most likely appear as nonsense on the recipient's mobile

[a7 2/2] telephone.

Before the message can be sent, one must determine the domain of the mobile carrier's SMS gateway. For example, if one wants
>> p! a7 22
[a7 1/2] to send a message to a mobile telephone in the United States serviced by AT&T, and the telephone number is +1 415-123-4567, the email would be

[a7 2/2] addressed as

4151234567@txt.att.net
To determine the SMS gateway domain, *e.g.*, txt.att.net, may require research - but most users
>> p! a7 23
[a7 1/2] know who their carrier is. The telephone number in this example for a US number is expressed as ten (10) digits, without the country code (1) and

[a7 2/2] without dashes or other separator characters when composing the email address. The country code is not needed, as the 10-digit telephone
>> p! a7 24
[a7 1/2] number, together with the email domain, are sufficient to send the email from any location in the world.

[a7 2/2] It is useful to perform a character count before sending the message to ensure that it is within the 160-character limit. If it exceeds
>> p! a7 25
[a7 1/2] the limit, the SMS gateway should break the message into a set of consecutive 160-character, or shorter, messages to the mobile equipment, although

[a7 2/2] breaks may occur in the middle of words.

A message sent with an email client can be simultaneously addressed to multiple mobile
>> p! a7 26
[a7 1/2] telephones - just as text messages sent in the usual manner between mobile telephones can be sent to multiple recipients.
